basic_information.name: EU Digital Omnibus on AI (Digital Omnibus Package)
basic_information.effective_date: Proposed 19 November 2025; if adopted, likely mid-2026 or later (subject to ordinary legislative procedure through European Parliament and Council trilogue)

scope_and_content.summary: The Digital Omnibus on AI is a European Commission legislative proposal published on 19 November 2025 to simplify the implementation of the EU AI Act. It is part of the broader Digital Omnibus Package, which also includes a Digital Omnibus amending the GDPR, ePrivacy Directive, NIS2, and Data Act. The AI Omnibus aims to reduce administrative burdens by at least 25% for all businesses and 35% for SMEs by 2029, by deferring high-risk AI compliance deadlines, extending SME relief to small mid-caps, softening AI literacy obligations, streamlining conformity assessments, and centralizing oversight under the AI Office.
key_provisions: Deferral of high-risk AI system obligations: Annex III systems delayed from August 2026 to December 2027 (max 16 months); Annex I systems delayed from August 2027 to August 2028 (max 24 months). Application is linked to Commission confirmation that harmonized standards and support measures are available, with 6 or 12 months lead time respectively.

AI literacy obligation shifted: No longer a direct obligation on providers and deployers; transformed into a duty for the Commission and Member States to encourage providers/deployers to take AI literacy measures.

Bias detection data processing: New Art. 4a allows providers and deployers of both high-risk and non-high-risk AI systems to process sensitive personal data for bias detection and correction, with the threshold lowered from 'strictly necessary' to 'necessary'.

SME/SMC regime extension: Simplified quality management system compliance (Art. 17) extended from microenterprises only to all SMEs and small mid-cap companies (SMCs, defined as <750 employees and <EUR 150M revenue). SMCs also receive privileged treatment in fine calculations.

Registration requirement removal: Providers of AI systems exempt from high-risk classification under Art. 6(3) no longer required to register in the EU database; only need to document a self-assessment.
Transparency obligation delay: Art. 50(2) obligations for AI-generated content marking/watermarking for systems placed on market before August 2026 delayed by 6 months to February 2027.

Centralized AI Office oversight: AI Office becomes exclusively competent for supervision and enforcement of AI systems based on GPAI models (where model and system share the same provider) and AI systems integrated into VLOPs/VLOSEs under the DSA.
Pre-market conformity assessments: Commission or entrusted notified bodies can organize pre-market conformity assessments for high-risk systems under AI Office supervision.

Sectoral conformity assessment priority: For dual-classified products (both Annex I.A and Annex III), the sectoral product law conformity assessment takes priority, with AI Act requirements integrated.
'Once-only' principle: Single application and assessment procedure for designation under both the AI Act and relevant sectoral legislation.
Expanded sandbox use: Possibility of EU-level AI regulatory sandbox operated by the AI Office; extended real-world testing for high-risk AI systems under Annex I (previously limited to Annex III).
Increased post-market monitoring flexibility: Removal of requirement for harmonized Commission template for post-market monitoring plans.
scope_and_content.risk_classification: The Omnibus does not change the fundamental risk-based classification structure of the AI Act (unacceptable/high/limited/minimal risk). It modifies how and when high-risk obligations are applied: deferring the application timeline, streamlining conformity assessments for dual-classified systems, and removing registration requirements for AI systems exempted from high-risk under Art. 6(3).
scope_and_content.covered_entities: Providers, deployers, importers, and distributors of AI systems operating in the EU market. Extended scope to small mid-cap companies (SMCs). The AI Office gains exclusive enforcement authority over GPAI-based systems and VLOP/VLOSE-integrated systems.
scope_and_content.sector_scope: Cross-sector horizontal regulation. Specific provisions address sectoral product legislation (medical devices, machinery via Annex I.A), critical infrastructure (Annex III), and platform regulation (VLOPs/VLOSEs under DSA). No new sector exemptions introduced.
scope_and_content.open_source_treatment: The Digital Omnibus on AI does not introduce specific new provisions regarding open-source AI models. The existing AI Act exemptions for open-source GPAI models remain unchanged: open-source GPAI providers are exempt from some documentation and representation obligations, but providers of open-source GPAI models with systemic risks remain subject to all obligations. The broader simplified compliance regime for SMEs and SMCs would benefit many open-source developers who fall within those categories.
scope_and_content.extraterritorial_reach: Maintains the AI Act's existing extraterritorial reach: the regulation applies to providers placing AI systems on the EU market or putting them into service in the EU, regardless of where they are established. Third-country providers of non-open-source GPAI models must still appoint an authorized representative in the EU. The Omnibus does not alter these provisions.

compliance_and_enforcement.penalties: The Omnibus does not change the AI Act's existing penalty tiers: Tier 1 (prohibited AI practices): up to EUR 35M or 7% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. Tier 2 (high-risk system violations): up to EUR 15M or 3% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. Tier 3 (misleading information): up to EUR 7.5M or 1% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. The Omnibus extends the SME fine calculation method to SMCs: for SMEs and SMCs, fines use the lower (not higher) of the fixed amount or percentage threshold, significantly reducing effective penalties for smaller companies.
compliance_and_enforcement.enforcement_body: The AI Office within the European Commission gains exclusive supervisory and enforcement competence for GPAI-based AI systems and VLOP/VLOSE-integrated systems. National market surveillance authorities retain competence for other AI systems. Conformity assessment bodies handle pre-market assessments.
compliance_and_enforcement.compliance_timeline: Original AI Act deadlines are modified as follows: Prohibited AI practices: 2 February 2025 (unchanged). AI literacy: obligation shifted to Commission/Member States (no firm deadline for providers). High-risk AI systems (Annex III): deferred from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 (backstop), or 6 months after Commission confirms support measures are available, whichever is earlier. High-risk AI systems (Annex I): deferred from 2 August 2027 to 2 August 2028 (backstop), or 12 months after Commission confirms support measures. Art. 50(2) transparency/marking for pre-August 2026 systems: deferred to 2 February 2027. Public authority compliance: 2 August 2030 (unchanged). Notified body AI Act designation: by 2 February 2028.
compliance_and_enforcement.reporting_requirements: The Omnibus retains existing AI Act reporting requirements for serious incidents by providers of high-risk AI systems. It removes the harmonized Commission template for post-market monitoring plans, allowing providers more flexibility. Self-assessment documentation replaces EU database registration for Art. 6(3) exempt systems. The broader Digital Omnibus Package introduces a single-entry EU portal for data breach reporting across GDPR, NIS2, DORA, and CER Directive.
compliance_and_enforcement.sme_provisions: Central pillar of the proposal. Key provisions: (1) Simplified quality management system compliance (Art. 17) extended from microenterprises to all SMEs and startups. (2) SME regulatory benefits (simplified technical documentation, sandbox access, support measures) extended to small mid-cap companies (SMCs: <750 employees, <EUR 150M revenue). (3) SMCs benefit from privileged fine calculation: lower of fixed amount or percentage threshold applies. (4) Quality management systems required proportionate to organization size. (5) Administrative burden reduction target of 35% for SMEs by 2029 (vs. 25% for all businesses). (6) Definitions of SMEs and SMCs aligned with previous Commission recommendations.

impact_and_analysis.business_impact: The Omnibus significantly benefits businesses of all sizes, but most directly aids SMEs and small mid-caps. (1) For large enterprises: The 16-24 month deferral of high-risk AI deadlines provides crucial additional compliance time, especially given that harmonized standards from CEN-CENELEC are not expected before Q4 2026. However, the substantive requirements remain unchanged, and businesses report needing at least 12 months to comply with a single standard. (2) For SMEs and startups: The extension of simplified compliance to all SMEs (not just micro-enterprises), proportionate quality management requirements, and reduced fine exposure provide meaningful relief. The estimated EUR 6B+ in administrative cost savings across all businesses and public administrations by 2029 disproportionately benefits smaller firms. (3) For small mid-caps (SMCs): A new category of beneficiary. Entities with <750 employees and <EUR 150M revenue now qualify for regulatory flexibilities previously reserved for SMEs, including simplified documentation and privileged fine treatment. (4) For AI system integrators: Centralized AI Office oversight and the 'once-only' conformity assessment principle reduce duplicative compliance processes. (5) Criticism: Morrison Foerster analysis notes that the Omnibus 'offers only limited substantive reductions' and that 'the strict sunset date for the suspension is problematic, particularly if the development of harmonized standards faces further delays.'
impact_and_analysis.innovation_effect: Mixed assessment. Promotes innovation through: deferred compliance deadlines allowing more development time; expanded regulatory sandbox access including an EU-level sandbox; extended real-world testing to Annex I high-risk systems; relaxed AI literacy obligations reducing administrative overhead; legitimate interest basis for personal data in AI training (via the broader Data Omnibus). However, critics argue: the Omnibus fails to expand the research exemption to real-world testing; it does not clarify key definitions like 'provider'; the fundamental rights impact assessment obligation remains, creating overlap with GDPR DPIAs; and Member States can still require consent for AI data processing, undermining harmonization. The Draghi Report context is key: the EU identified an innovation gap vis-a-vis the US and China in advanced technologies, and the Omnibus is a direct response.
impact_and_analysis.global_influence: The Omnibus represents a notable shift in EU regulatory philosophy. While the EU pioneered comprehensive AI regulation with the AI Act (entering force August 2024), the Omnibus signals a recalibration toward competitiveness. This follows a broader international trend: the US Trump Administration adopted a deregulatory approach under its 'AI Arms Race' policy, and the UK passed its Data (Use and Access) Act 2024 with pragmatic simplifications. The 'Brussels Effect' dynamic is evolving: rather than other jurisdictions racing to match EU strictness, the EU is now partially retreating from its own regulatory ambitions. However, the Commission insists this is 'simplification, not softening of standards.' The GDPR-related changes in the broader Data Omnibus may influence other jurisdictions that modeled their data protection laws on the GDPR. The UK ICO's pragmatic approach may welcome similar simplifications.
impact_and_analysis.stakeholder_positions: Sharply divided. SUPPORTERS: DigitalEurope welcomed the delays and business wallet as crucial competitiveness steps. MEP Eva Maydell (EPP) framed it as industrial survival. The Commission projects EUR 6B+ savings. Many businesses welcome the AI Act delays given the absence of harmonized standards. CRITICS: NOYB (Max Schrems) called it 'the biggest attack on Europeans digital rights in years' and said it 'would mainly benefit Big Tech.' 127 civil society organizations signed a critical joint statement. BEUC warned that processing personal data for AI without consent gives large firms an advantage over European startups. MEP Alex Agius Saliba (S&D) said it 'could recklessly undermine the EU digital legal framework.' MEP Kim van Sparrentak (Greens-EFA) warned of 'rolling out the red carpet to a business model based on stolen data.' The EDPB and EDPS challenged the claim that changes are only minor modifications, noting the personal data definition change goes further than CJEU case law. CDT Europe raised concerns about weakened oversight.
impact_and_analysis.deregulatory_signals: Strong deregulatory signal, though the Commission frames it as 'simplification.' Specific mechanisms: (1) Deferral of high-risk compliance deadlines by 16-24 months. (2) Removal of AI literacy obligations from providers/deployers. (3) Removal of registration requirements for Art. 6(3) exempt systems. (4) Lowered threshold for sensitive data processing from 'strictly necessary' to 'necessary.' (5) Extended relief categories (SMCs). (6) Removal of harmonized post-market monitoring template. (7) The broader Data Omnibus adds GDPR simplifications (cookie consent reform, narrowed personal data definition, legitimate interest for AI training). The Digital Fitness Check consultation (open until 11 March 2026) signals further potential deregulation. The Omnibus is explicitly a response to the Draghi Report's competitiveness concerns and the perceived innovation gap with the US and China.

related_regulations: Regulation 2018/1139 (EASA aviation regulation, also amended by the AI Omnibus)
connections_and_context.key_actors: European Commission (proposer): Executive VP Henna Virkkunen (digital portfolio), Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath (GDPR aspects). Legislative co-legislators: European Parliament, Council of the EU. Key MEPs: Eva Maydell (EPP, supportive), Alex Agius Saliba (S&D, critical), Kim van Sparrentak (Greens-EFA, critical). Enforcement: AI Office (within Commission), national market surveillance authorities. Standardization: CEN-CENELEC Joint Technical Committee 21 (drafting harmonized AI standards). Advisory: EDPB, EDPS (both cautious about scope of changes). Civil society: NOYB/Max Schrems (strongly opposed), BEUC (consumer protection concerns), CDT Europe (AI governance concerns), 127 civil society organizations (joint critical statement). Industry: DigitalEurope (supportive). Contextual: Mario Draghi (author of the competitiveness report that motivated the Omnibus).
recent_developments: 19 November 2025: European Commission published the Digital Omnibus Package, comprising the AI Omnibus (COM(2025) 836) and the Digital Omnibus (COM(2025) 837), along with the Data Union Strategy and European Business Wallets.
November-December 2025: Eight-week feedback period opened; being extended daily until available in all EU languages (initially until 29 January 2026).
December 2025: EDPB and EDPS challenged the scope of changes, particularly the personal data definition revision.
127 civil society organizations published joint criticism of the proposals.
11 March 2026 deadline: Digital Fitness Check consultation closes; this comprehensive 'stress test' of the Digital Rulebook may lead to further simplification proposals.
2 February 2026: Commission missed its own deadline for publishing Art. 6 guidance on high-risk AI systems classification.
CEN-CENELEC indicated harmonized AI standards may not be available before Q4 2026.
European Parliament and Council began ordinary legislative procedure review; adoption likely mid-2026 or later, with possibility of accelerated procedure.
Commission also issued parallel guidance on serious incident reporting for high-risk AI and practical application of high-risk requirements.

teaching_relevance.entrepreneurial_implications: Highly relevant for AI entrepreneurs in France and the EU. Key implications: (1) Compliance timing: The 16-24 month deferral of high-risk AI deadlines gives startups more runway to develop products before facing compliance obligations, but the requirements themselves are not reduced. (2) Cost reduction: The extension of simplified compliance to all SMEs and SMCs means most startups benefit from lighter quality management, simplified documentation, and proportionate requirements -- not just micro-enterprises. Fine exposure is also reduced (lower-of threshold). (3) Market access: The 'once-only' conformity assessment and centralized AI Office oversight simplify market entry for GPAI-based products. (4) Data advantage: The broader Data Omnibus's legitimate interest basis for AI training data gives EU startups more flexibility to train models on personal data, though critics warn this mainly benefits Big Tech. (5) Competitive moat: The regulatory sandbox expansion, including an EU-level sandbox, creates opportunities for startups to test high-risk AI in controlled environments. (6) Strategic risk: The Omnibus is still a proposal under legislative review; startups should not assume final rules will match the proposal. The ongoing Digital Fitness Check could bring further changes. (7) French/European context: The Omnibus responds to the Draghi Report on EU competitiveness and directly addresses concerns that EU regulation is driving innovation to the US and China. Mistral AI and similar EU AI companies benefit from the deferral and simplified compliance. (8) Discussion question: 'If you are building a high-risk AI system, should you delay compliance efforts or start now despite the proposed deferral?'

confidence.cross_reference: Information confirmed across multiple authoritative sources: Morrison Foerster client alert (1 Dec 2025), Skadden first impressions (Nov 2025), Crowell & Moring client alert (1 Dec 2025), IAPP analysis (9 Dec 2025), Sidley Austin analysis (Dec 2025), Cooley analysis (Nov 2025), Latham & Watkins analysis (Dec 2025), PWC analysis, official EC press release (IP/25/2718), and Kennedys Law analysis (Jan 2026). All sources are consistent on the core provisions. Official legislative text: COM(2025) 836 final (AI Omnibus) and COM(2025) 837 final (Data Omnibus).
confidence.caveats: This is a Commission proposal under the ordinary legislative procedure; the final text will be negotiated by the European Parliament and Council and is likely to change substantially. The AI Act's underlying requirements are not simplified, only deferred. The harmonized standards from CEN-CENELEC are still under development. The Digital Fitness Check (open until 11 March 2026) could lead to further proposals. Some of the most impactful changes (GDPR personal data definition, legitimate interest for AI training) are in the separate Data Omnibus, not the AI Omnibus itself. Civil society opposition is strong and may influence Parliament's position. The Commission missed its own 2 February deadline for Art. 6 guidance, raising questions about implementation capacity.
